levels.title: Small rivers, one rule at a time
levels.theory: Bruner's spiral curriculum, because the learner first sees a one-off mapping as a concrete situation, then revisits it as a general idea, then meets the named abstraction, then applies that abstraction again on new data.
levels.designNote: A field assistant measuring tributary inflow needs a throwaway conversion rule per river, which is exactly when a lambda fits, and the level boundary is the moment the learner stops writing def blocks for one-line transforms.

caseStudies.scenario: Maya is a hydrology field assistant in the Okavango Delta. Her supervisor asked for the average discharge of every tributary they sampled this week, converted from cubic meters per second into cubic kilometers per year. Each river has its own reading, and she has to hand the supervisor a one-line summary before tomorrow's briefing. She wrote a tiny rule for each tributary by hand, but the list grew past thirty entries and the copy-paste approach is starting to crack.

stage1.prompt: Here are three of Maya's raw readings, each followed by the converted value she typed by hand: Zambezi chunk: 1.20 m^3/s turns into 0.0378 km^3/yr. Cuando chunk: 0.45 m^3/s turns into 0.0142 km^3/yr. Linyanti chunk: 0.08 m^3/s turns into 0.0025 km^3/yr.
stage1.guidingQuestion: What do you notice about how each raw number is being turned into the converted number?

attempt1.text: Each raw reading is being multiplied by the same fixed amount to produce the converted reading.
Each raw reading is being divided by the river's name length to produce the converted reading.
attempt1.hint: If that were true, the Cuando and Zambezi readings would scale with the number of letters in the river name. Look at the three pairs and try the same rule on each.

attempt1.text: Each reading is being converted by subtracting the average of the other two readings.
attempt1.hint: Try applying that rule to the Zambezi pair and see if it produces 0.0378. The rule has to hold for all three, not just feel plausible for one.

stage3.conceptIdea: A small unnamed rule that takes one number in and hands back a transformed number, written in a single line wherever it is needed rather than given a name of its own.

stage4.conceptReveal: Python calls this a lambda function: a one-line anonymous rule, written with lambda, given its inputs, a single expression, and used wherever a small transform is needed.
stage4.codeTemplate:
convert = ___ x: x * ___

readings = [1.20, 0.45, 0.08]
yearly = list(map(___, readings))
print(yearly)

tokens.hint: def opens a named block that needs more than one line. Maya wants a throwaway one-line rule.
That number is the seconds in a year, but the raw readings are already in m^3/s and the targets are in km^3/yr, so the multiplier has to fold both unit jumps in at once.
Passing the whole list here would give the rule a list to multiply, which is not what map needs.

flowSteps.label: Python evaluates the right-hand side first.
flowSteps.note: lambda x: x * 0.031536 creates a tiny rule that waits for a number.

flowSteps.label: That rule is stored in the name convert.
flowSteps.note: It still has not been called on anything yet.

flowSteps.label: map hands each reading to convert, one at a time.
flowSteps.note: 1.20, then 0.45, then 0.08 each get multiplied by 0.031536.

flowSteps.label: list() collects the three results in order.
print writes that list.
flowSteps.note: The supervisor sees all three converted readings on one line.

options.hint: Those are Maya's hand-typed values. The actual multiplication 1.20 * 0.031536 produces more decimals than she wrote down.
map wrapped in list(...) gives a list, not a space-separated string.

edgeCase.question: What if the lambda line is removed and convert is used directly in map without ever being defined?

options.text: Python raises NameError when map tries to look up convert.
Python silently treats the missing rule as identity and prints the raw readings.
options.hint: Python does not guess what an undefined name should mean. Think about what happens when a name has no binding.

options.text: Python runs the map call but skips every reading and prints an empty list.
options.hint: The reading loop never gets a chance to run because the name lookup fails before map starts.

stage5.practicePrompt: A second station reports the tributary widths in meters, and Maya now needs a one-line rule that turns each width into kilometers and rounds to two decimals before the briefing. Use a lambda with map.

practiceTokens.hint: A def block wants a name and its own lines. The task asks for a one-line rule.
int would chop off the decimals instead of rounding to two places.
Dividing meters by that number would still leave meters, not kilometers.

applyCheck.prompt: Which of these is a real fit for writing the rule as a one-line lambda rather than a def block?

options.text: Sorting a long list of tributary readings from highest to lowest discharge.
options.hint: Sorting is a built-in operation, not a small unnamed rule you write yourself.

options.text: Computing one-off area under a hydrograph for a single week's samples.
Storing the full team roster and their contact phone numbers for the whole season.
options.hint: A roster is data to keep, not a one-line transform. A def block or a plain dict fits that better.

caseStudies.scaleReflection: When Maya's list grows from thirty tributaries to three hundred, what changes about why writing each rule as a one-line lambda is the right choice over copy-pasting by hand?

levels.title: The Pilgrim's Ledger
levels.theory: Bruner's spiral curriculum, because the learner meets a pattern in a concrete temple inventory, returns to the same shape in stage5 with a different ask, and each pass deepens the abstraction from observation to syntax to independent use.
levels.designNote: Levels (foundation then applied) because first the learner sees the pattern of pulling filtered records out of a temple ledger, then applies that same shaping to a different ask about the same archive. The boundary sits at 'can the learner write the shape on their own,' not at richer syntax.
levels.domain: The Great Indian Temples and the built stories behind them

caseStudies.scenario: Anika runs a small heritage homestay in Thanjavur and keeps a hand-written ledger of every pilgrim who stayed with her during the Brihadeeswara temple festival season. She needs to send a single printed sheet to the temple trust by Friday morning listing only the devotees who visited on the third day of the festival, and the ledger already has 230 entries.

stage1.prompt: Anika flips open her ledger. The pages are ruled into neat columns: name, village, day visited, donation amount. On day 3 alone there are forty-one rows. She runs her finger down the 'day visited' column, then across each row, copying names onto a separate sheet of paper.
stage1.guidingQuestion: What is Anika doing to the ledger, row by row, that takes her a long time by hand?

attempt1.text: Going through each row and pulling out only the ones she wants onto a new sheet.
Reading the whole ledger once and remembering the day-3 names without writing them down.
attempt1.hint: If 230 entries arrived and she had to add day-4 names too, would her memory hold up? Try writing each one down instead of trusting your head.

attempt1.text: Recopying every single row, including the day-1 and day-2 pilgrims, onto the new sheet.
attempt1.hint: The trust asked for only day-3 visitors. What happens to the paper Anika hands over if it includes everyone?

stage3.conceptIdea: A short way to take a whole collection, keep only the items that match a rule, and reshape each kept item into a new list, all in one step.

stage4.conceptReveal: Python calls this shape a list comprehension: an expression applied to every item in a collection, with an optional condition, all written inside square brackets.

tokens.hint: This phrase is two of the missing pieces joined together. Fill each blank with one small word so the square brackets read cleanly.
That's the whole filtering clause squashed into one chunk. Each blank wants a single short word that sits between the other pieces.
That belongs on the left side of the equals sign, not inside the brackets.

flowSteps.label: Python looks at ledger, the collection of all 230 pilgrim rows.
It pulls out one pilgrim at a time and assigns it to pilgrim.
It checks whether pilgrim["day"] is equal to 3. Rows that fail are skipped.
For each row that passes, it grabs pilgrim["name"] and collects it.
All collected names are bundled into the new list and bound to day_3_names.
print(day_3_names) writes the day-3 names to the screen for Anika to copy onto her sheet.

predictOutput.question: The ledger contains pilgrims from day 1 through day 5. What does this code print?

options.text: A list of just the names of the forty-one pilgrims whose "day" value is 3.
A list of every pilgrim's name from all five days, since the ledger holds them all.
options.hint: The condition inside the brackets decides who makes the cut. Names from days 1, 2, 4, and 5 don't satisfy it.

options.text: The number 41, since that is how many day-3 rows the ledger has.
options.hint: The expression before 'for' is the thing collected, not a count of matches.

edgeCase.question: What happens if Anika forgets to include the 'if pilgrim["day"] == 3' part of the comprehension?

options.text: Every pilgrim's name from all 230 rows ends up in day_3_names, even day-1 and day-5 visitors.
Python raises an error because the comprehension is missing a required piece.
options.hint: The 'if' clause is optional in Python. Without it, the comprehension still runs, just without filtering.

options.text: day_3_names stays empty, since no rule is telling Python which rows to keep.
options.hint: Without a filter, the default behavior is to keep everything, not nothing.

stage5.practicePrompt: The temple trust now asks Anika for a second sheet: only the names of pilgrims who gave a donation of 500 rupees or more, regardless of which day they visited. Write a list comprehension that pulls those names out of the same ledger.

practiceTokens.hint: 500 is a floor, not an exact match. Think about whether 500 rupees counts or only amounts equal to 500.
That's two of the blanks fused into one. Each blank takes a single short word.
That's the whole filtering clause as one chunk. Break it apart so each blank gets one small piece.
That lives on the left side of the equals sign, not inside the brackets.

applyCheck.prompt: Which of these is another task where the same shaping of a collection fits naturally?

options.text: From a list of every train that left Chennai Egmore last week, pull out only the train numbers that were delayed.
Look up the price of one specific sari that a customer is asking about today.
options.hint: That's pulling a single item out of a collection, not reshaping every item into a new list.

options.text: Write down the total number of pilgrims in the ledger without naming any of them.
options.hint: That asks for a single count, not a new list built from the ledger's rows.

caseStudies.scaleReflection: If Anika's ledger grew from 230 entries to 2,300 next festival season, would the comprehension still finish the job in a single run the way her hand-copying could not?

levels.title: Tiny rules for tiny moments
levels.theory: Bruner's spiral curriculum, because the learner first notices sorting rivers by an improvised rule, then sees the underlying idea of a tiny throwaway rule, then returns to a richer list later in stage5 to apply that same idea at a larger scale.
levels.designNote: Aanya is classifying Indian rivers by a single shifting trait for her journal, so the rule is short-lived and changes often; lambda is the right fit because any full def would be heavier than the rule itself. One level only: lambda has no structural siblings that force a different shape, only the choice between using one or naming a def instead.
levels.domain: Indian River and the stories behind them

caseStudies.scenario: Aanya runs a weekend journal called 'Rivers I Have Known,' and for tomorrow's entry she is sorting twelve Indian rivers by their length in kilometers. She expects to redo the sort next week by catchment area, then the week after by the year they were first mapped, so she wants the rule to be small and replaceable each time.

stage1.prompt: Here is the list she is about to sort: [('Krishna', 1400), ('Godavari', 1465), ('Kaveri', 800), ('Yamuna', 1370), ('Narmada', 1310), ('Tapi', 724)]. The numbers are lengths in kilometers.
stage1.guidingQuestion: If Aanya wants this list ordered shortest river first, what does she actually need to tell the sort?

attempt1.text: A small one-line rule that looks at the second item of each pair and says 'use this for ordering.'
A full named function that compares rivers by name first and falls back to length.
attempt1.hint: She is re-sorting every week by a different trait. What happens to that named function the second week?

attempt1.text: A loop that walks the list, finds the shortest river, moves it to the front, and repeats.
attempt1.hint: The list is already going into Python's sort. What does Python need from her, not a replacement for the sort?

stage3.conceptIdea: A tiny, unnamed rule that takes an input and hands back the single value the sorter should use, written in one line because it will be replaced next week anyway.

stage4.conceptReveal: That's a lambda: a tiny anonymous function written on one line, perfect for a rule you'll throw away next week.

flowSteps.label: Python sees the rivers list
flowSteps.note: It holds six tuples, each a river name and its length in kilometers.

flowSteps.label: Python reads the key argument
flowSteps.note: It notices a small rule attached to the sort, not a named function.

flowSteps.label: For each tuple, Python calls the rule
flowSteps.note: It hands the whole pair to the lambda's parameter.

flowSteps.label: The rule returns the length
flowSteps.note: It pulls out index 1, the number, and gives that back to the sort.

flowSteps.label: Python sorts using those numbers
flowSteps.note: Pairs get ordered shortest to longest, and the print line shows the full pairs.

predictOutput.question: When the code runs, which line does it print?

options.hint: Kaveri is 800 km and Tapi is 724 km. Which one is shorter?

options.text: It prints only the river names, not the numbers.
options.hint: The list still holds full pairs after sort. What does print(rivers) show?

edgeCase.question: What happens if Aanya leaves out the word 'lambda' and just writes key=pair: pair[1]?

options.text: Python raises a SyntaxError because it doesn't know what kind of rule this is.
Python guesses she meant a lambda and sorts anyway.
options.hint: Python doesn't guess. What word marks the start of a tiny rule?

options.text: The list ends up in alphabetical order by river name.
options.hint: Without the rule, sort has nothing to compare on. Would it even run?

stage5.practicePrompt: Next week's journal entry is ready. Sort the same rivers by their catchment area in square kilometers: [('Krishna', 258948), ('Godavari', 312812), ('Kaveri', 81155), ('Yamuna', 366223), ('Narmada', 98796), ('Tapi', 65145)]. Use the same kind of tiny one-line rule.

applyCheck.prompt: Which of these jobs is a tiny throwaway rule the right tool for?

options.text: Telling sorted() to order students by the third letter of their name for a one-off quiz seating chart.
Building a full gradebook report that's reused every term for every class.
options.hint: If it's reused every term, is 'throwaway' still the right shape?

options.text: Writing a login check that validates usernames across the whole app.
options.hint: A login check runs in lots of places. Would a one-line rule still be there to read later?

caseStudies.scaleReflection: If Aanya's list grew from six rivers to two hundred across many regions, would a tiny one-line rule still be enough to tell the sort what to order by?

levels.title: The Landslide Notice
levels.theory: Kolb's experiential cycle: the learner first observes a raw failure (stage1), interprets what went wrong (stage2), forms a general idea about catching failures before they crash the program (stage3), builds the concrete Python mechanism for it (stage4), and applies it to a fresh situation (stage5). Each beat is one phase of the cycle, so reflection and active experimentation are inseparable.
levels.designNote: Anita has to keep posting village advisories even when one report breaks the pipeline, so the scenario lives entirely inside the moment where a missing file or a bad number would crash her script, and beginner level is set at a single try/except pair with no chaining or custom exceptions because the concrete trap is just learning that one failure shouldn't end the whole run.
levels.domain: Indian mountains and the stories behind it

caseStudies.scenario: Anita runs the notice board at a small information centre in Mukteshwar, and every evening she posts a short advisory for the next day's trekkers based on three reports she gets by email: road status from the block office, weather from a met tower, and a landslide risk note from the district portal. Yesterday one of those emails was malformed, her script blew up on the bad row, and the morning board went blank, so the dayhikers left without knowing the trail past Chestnut Hill was washed out. Tonight she needs to rebuild the script so a single bad report cannot blank out the whole advisory.

stage1.prompt:
Here is what Anita's old script printed last night when it crashed:

Reading road status... OK
Reading weather... OK
Reading landslide note... ERROR: could not convert 'N/A' to integer

The board stopped there. No combined advisory was posted.
stage1.guidingQuestion: What do you notice about where the script gave up, and what never got written to the board as a result?

attempt1.text: It gave up on the very first report that broke, so everything coming after that report was lost with it.
It gave up only on the landslide report and left the road and weather lines blank on the board.
attempt1.hint: If the whole board was blank, what does that say about whether the earlier two reports ever reached the wall?

attempt1.text: It posted a partial advisory with whatever it had already read, and just skipped the broken line.
attempt1.hint: If a partial advisory had gone up, Anita would not be calling the script a failure today. What did she actually see on the board?

stage3.conceptIdea: A way to mark one step as risky, decide in advance what to do if that step blows up, and then keep going with the rest of the work instead of letting the failure end the whole job.

stage4.conceptReveal: Python's way of doing this is a try/except block: wrap the risky step in `try`, give `except` instructions for what to do if that step blows up, and the script keeps running after the crash.
stage4.codeTemplate:
reports = {
    "road": read_road(),
    "weather": read_weather(),
    "landslide": read_landslide()
}

for name, value in reports.items():
    ___:
        post(name, value)
    ___ ValueError:
        post(name, "Report unavailable — check back later.")

print("Advisory posted.")

tokens.hint: An `if` only checks a condition you write yourself. It cannot catch a crash from inside a function call.
`finally` runs no matter what, but it doesn't decide what to do when the step blows up.
`raise` creates a new failure instead of handling one that already happened.
A loop just repeats. It won't change what happens when the line inside it crashes.

flowSteps.label: Loop starts on the first report (road).
flowSteps.note: Python enters the loop with name='road', value=the road status.

flowSteps.label: Python tries to post the road status.
flowSteps.note: The `try` block runs post('road', value). It succeeds, so the `except` block is skipped.

flowSteps.label: Loop moves on to the weather report.
flowSteps.note: Same thing happens: post('weather', value) works, except is skipped.

flowSteps.label: Loop reaches the landslide report, and read_landslide() returns 'N/A'.
flowSteps.note: Inside `try`, the call to post() tries to convert 'N/A' to an integer and raises ValueError.

flowSteps.label: Python jumps to the matching except block.
flowSteps.note: Instead of crashing the whole script, it runs post('landslide', 'Report unavailable...').

flowSteps.label: Loop ends, and the final print runs.
flowSteps.note: All three advisories are on the board, even though one was bad — 'Advisory posted.' prints.

predictOutput.question: With Anita's three reports where the landslide value is 'N/A', what ends up on the board when this script runs?

options.text: Road status, weather, landslide advisory, then 'Advisory posted.'
Just the road and weather lines, then a crash message.
options.hint: The except block replaces the crash with a fallback message, so the landslide line still gets written.

options.text: Only 'Report unavailable — check back later.' for the landslide.
options.hint: The earlier two reports are fine, so their except blocks are never entered.

edgeCase.question: What happens if Anita forgets to write the `except` line and only keeps `try`?

options.text: Python refuses to run the script at all because `try` has no partner.
The script runs fine and just skips any bad report silently.
options.hint: Skipping a bad report is what the except line does. Without it, what catches the crash?

options.text: The script runs but only handles the first report.
options.hint: The loop would still run three times — the issue is whether the bad one is caught, not how many run.

stage5.practicePrompt: A tea shop owner in the same village asks Anita to total the day's sales from a file where each line is a number, but at least one line is a stray word like 'closed'. Help her write a small loop that totals the numbers and treats any line that can't be turned into a number as zero.
stage5.practiceTemplate:
total = 0
for line in open("sales.txt"):
    ___:
        total += int(line)
    ___ ValueError:
        total += 0

print("Today's total:", total)

practiceTokens.hint: An `if` cannot catch the crash that happens inside `int(line)` when the line is a word.
`elif` only chains another condition onto an `if` — it doesn't catch a raised error.
`finally` always runs, but it doesn't decide what to do when the step blows up.
`raise` makes a new error. We want to absorb one that already happened.

applyCheck.prompt: Which of these is a real case for try/except, not something a plain if could solve?

options.text: Reading a customer name from a form and checking if the field is empty before saving.
options.hint: An empty field is predictable — a plain `if` checks it before any crash happens.

options.text: Opening a settings file at startup that might not exist on a fresh install, and falling back to defaults.
Adding a 10% discount only when the cart total is over a certain amount.
options.hint: That's a normal comparison — no crash is involved, so no try/except needed.

caseStudies.scaleReflection: If Anita's report list grew from 3 sources to 200, and a few bad values were scattered through them, how would the same try/except pattern let her board still go up with every good report visible?

levels.title: The Name on the Jar
levels.designNote: Miles Morales needs to reuse the same guest count across several sentences in a poster draft, which makes 'a name that holds a value' the right concept for him to meet now. Justified by Piaget: he is dealing with concrete numbers on paper before any formal symbol can mean anything to him.

caseStudies.scenario: Miles Morales is drafting a poster for the Brooklyn Visions Academy open mic night. He keeps rewriting 'this Friday, 47 students signed up, and 47 students means...' on the chalkboard and smudging it. His friend Ganke asked him to text the final count before dinner, and Miles wants the poster to stay clean enough to photograph.

stage1.prompt: On the chalkboard, Miles has written: '47 students signed up. 47 students will perform. 47 students need chairs. Bring 47 friends!' He is about to erase one of those numbers and rewrite it, but Ganke texts asking for the count again.
stage1.guidingQuestion: What is the part that stays the same in every one of those sentences, and what would happen if Miles had to change that number on the poster?

attempt1.text: Miles picks one short name and uses it in place of the number in every sentence, so changing the number only happens in one place.
Miles copies the number four times and erases each one separately whenever the count changes.
attempt1.hint: What if 200 students signed up instead of 47, and Miles had to find and fix every copy on a crowded chalkboard?

attempt1.text: Miles stops writing the number on the poster at all and just says 'a lot of students' in every sentence.
attempt1.hint: Ganke asked for the actual count before dinner. How would 'a lot' help him text it back?

stage3.conceptIdea: A short name that stands in for a value, so the value lives in one place and every sentence that needs it points back to that same name.

stage4.conceptReveal: In Python, that short name that stands in for a value is called a variable. You write it with the name on the left, an equals sign, then the value.
stage4.codeTemplate:
students = ___
print(students, "students signed up.")
print(students, "students will perform.")
print(students, "students need chairs.")

tokens.hint: If the value were the name itself, what number would get printed?
Quotes would make it a piece of text, not a number Miles could change with arithmetic later.

flowSteps.label: Line 1 runs first: Python sees the name students, then the equals sign, then 47.
flowSteps.note: Python stores 47 under the name students, like writing a label on a jar.

flowSteps.label: Line 2 runs: Python looks up students, finds 47, and prints 47 students signed up.
Line 3 runs: Python looks up students again, still finds 47, and prints 47 students will perform.
Line 4 runs: same lookup, same value, prints 47 students need chairs.
If Miles later writes students = 200 on line 1, every print below it would say 200 instead.
flowSteps.note: One change in one place updates every sentence that uses the name.

predictOutput.question: If Miles runs this code as written, what does it print?

options.text:
47 students signed up.
47 students will perform.
47 students need chairs.

students students signed up.
students students will perform.
students students need chairs.
options.hint: Each print uses the name, and the name points to a number. Which one actually gets printed?

options.text: Only one line: 47 students signed up.
options.hint: There are three separate print statements. Each one runs in order.

edgeCase.question: What happens if Miles forgets the equals sign and writes students 47 instead?

options.text: Python gives a SyntaxError because students 47 is not valid code.
Python guesses that students and 47 should be the same and runs anyway.
options.hint: Python does not guess. Two words sitting next to each other with no equals sign have no meaning to it.

options.text: Python treats it as the number 47 but ignores the word students.
options.hint: Why would Python quietly drop the name Miles meant to use?

stage5.practicePrompt: Ganke texts back: 'wait, also tell me how many chairs we need if every performer brings one parent.' Miles has to compute 47 students plus 47 parents using a variable, then print the total.
stage5.practiceTemplate:
students = ___
parents = ___
total = ___
print("We need", total, "chairs.")

practiceTokens.hint: students already holds 47. What name should hold the parent count instead?
parents should hold 47. But is 47 the right value for the line that computes the total?
total is where the sum goes, not where the inputs go.

applyCheck.prompt: Which of these is another situation where a short name standing in for one value would actually help?

options.text: A baker writes a recipe card and uses the same oven temperature in three sentences.
A reader finishes a novel once and never looks at it again.
options.hint: Is the value being reused, or used exactly once?

options.text: A friend tells you their name one time in conversation.
options.hint: Would you need a stored name for this, or just to hear it once?

caseStudies.scaleReflection: If 500 students signed up instead of 47, how many places on the poster would you have to change if you had used a name like students instead of copying the number everywhere?

levels.title: Level 1: Variables
levels.designNote: Anchored in Piaget's concrete-to-formal progression because the learner starts by observing a named character attach a real object to a name, then generalizes that experience into the formal rule that a name points to a value. The single level exists because introducing a second concept (reassignment, types, etc.) would force a separate cognitive jump that this stage cannot absorb.

caseStudies.scenario: Maya runs the snack booth at her little brother's school carnival, and she owes her abuela a handwritten list of how many churros, elotes, and aguas frescas she sold by Saturday. The stand is chaotic, and every time someone shouts an order she scribbles it on a napkin that someone then wipes a counter with. Her abuela calls Friday night to ask, '¿ya tienes los números?' and Maya still has nothing pinned down.

stage1.prompt: Maya writes down three napkins: one says 'churros,' one says 'elotes,' one says 'aguas frescas.' Every time someone orders one, she puts a tally mark on that napkin. By Friday night she can look at a napkin and know its number.
stage1.guidingQuestion: What is the napkin doing for Maya that her shouting memory cannot?

attempt1.text: Each napkin is a labeled container that holds one running count, so Maya can look it up by name instead of remembering every shout in her head.
The napkin is mainly a pretty decoration that makes the booth feel festive.
attempt1.hint: If the napkin were just decoration, would throwing one away change what Maya owes her abuela?

attempt1.text: The napkin only matters once the carnival ends, so Maya could wait until Sunday and tally everything from memory.
attempt1.hint: If orders were still being shouted on Sunday, what would Maya be missing?

stage3.conceptIdea: A name that points to a single piece of information you can update and read back whenever you need it, instead of holding the whole stream of shouts in your head.

stage4.conceptReveal: In Python, that napkin is called a variable: a name bound to a value that you can update and read back.
stage4.codeTemplate:
___ = 0
___ = 0
___ = 0
churros = churros + 1
elotes = elotes + 1
aguas_frescas = aguas_frescas + 1
print(churros, elotes, aguas_frescas)

tokens.hint: Maya's abuela didn't ask about tacos, and there's no tally for them on the napkins.
One napkin holds one running count, not a sum of all three.

flowSteps.label: Python creates three named values, each starting at 0
An order for a churro runs the line that reads the current churros count and writes back one more
An order for an elote does the same thing for the elotes name
An order for an aguas fresca does the same thing for the aguas_frescas name
Friday night, Maya reads all three names and the latest counts print out

predictOutput.question: After one churro, one elote, and two aguas frescas are ordered, what does the print line show?

options.hint: Those would be the starting counts, but orders have come in since then.
Each name tracks its own count, not a shared total.

edgeCase.question: What if Maya left out the first three lines that set each name to 0?

options.text: Python complains that churros, elotes, and aguas_frescas don't point to anything yet, so the +1 lines can't run.
Python quietly assumes each one is 0 and keeps going.
options.hint: Python won't invent a value for a name it's never seen.

options.text: All three counts end up stuck at 1 forever.
options.hint: The counts wouldn't move at all if the +1 lines failed.

stage5.practicePrompt: Maya's abuela also wants to know how much peso she started the booth with. Help Maya pin down a starting_cash name and a starting_cash value.

practiceTokens.hint: That's a snack count, not the peso amount Maya started with.
Quoting it would make it a label, not a number Maya can do math on later.

applyCheck.prompt: Which of these is another place where pinning one name to one updatable piece of information helps?

options.text: Tracking how many pages you've read in a book by writing today's count next to the book's title on a sticky note.
Reading a novel cover to cover in one sitting so you don't need to remember any of it.
options.hint: That's avoiding the problem of holding a running fact, not solving it with a name.

options.text: Memorizing your best friend's phone number once and never writing it anywhere.
options.hint: If the number changed, you'd have nothing pinned down to update.

caseStudies.scaleReflection: If Maya's abuela also wanted totals for horchata, tamales, and nachos next week, would adding three more names still feel manageable, or would you want a different way to organize them?

levels.title: Kofi's Notebook: Two Ways to Repeat
levels.theory: Kolb's experiential cycle, because the learner starts with concrete notebook data, reflects on what differs between the two entries, abstracts the general rule, and only later tests it by building code.
levels.designNote: The scenario needs two genuinely different reasons to repeat an action: a fixed known count and an unknown count driven by a target, so the boundary between the two ideas stays sharp instead of blurry. One level is enough here because the whole point is a single either/or decision, not a progression of difficulty.

caseStudies.scenario: Kofi Boateng runs a mobile phone-credit stand outside Kaneshie Market in Accra. Every morning before opening, he tops up credit for exactly 8 regular customers who prepaid the night before, working straight down his notebook list. During the day, when someone pays with a big note, he counts loose coins from his cash box into their hand one at a time until the change reaches the exact amount owed. He never knows ahead of time how many coins that will take, since it depends on what note they hand him and what they bought.

stage1.prompt: Here is a page from Kofi's notebook: a numbered list of his 8 morning customers, and beside it, a tally he scratched out while counting coins for Ama, one mark per coin, six marks total, stopping the moment the pile hit 13 cedis.
stage1.guidingQuestion: Look at how Kofi knows when to stop in each case. What's different?

attempt1.text: In the customer list he stops after the 8th name no matter what; with the coins he stops whenever the pile reaches 13 cedis, whether that takes 4 coins or 14.
Both are just Kofi repeating an action several times until he's done, so there's no real difference between them.
attempt1.hint: If Ama had paid with a note that needed 40 coins instead of 6, would counting them work the same way as going down a fixed list of 8 names?

attempt1.text: The customer list involves repeating an action, but counting coins is just one single action, not something that repeats.
attempt1.hint: If it takes six separate coins dropped one by one to reach 13 cedis, is that really only one action?

stage3.conceptIdea: There are two basic ways to repeat a set of steps: one where you know the exact number of rounds before you start, like going through a list, and one where you keep going only as long as some condition stays true, like counting coins until you hit an amount, where you only find out how many rounds it took after you stop.

stage4.conceptReveal: Python has two different tools for this: a for loop walks through a known sequence a fixed number of times, and a while loop keeps going only as long as a condition stays true.
stage4.codeTemplate:
customers = ["Ama", "Kwame", "Yaw", "Efua", "Kojo", "Abena", "Kwabena", "Adjoa"]
___ name in customers:
    top_up(name)

change_given = 0
coins_used = 0
___ change_given < 13:
    change_given += 2
    coins_used += 1

tokens.hint: What if Kofi doesn't know in advance how many coins it will take, only that he must keep going while the pile is still short?

flowSteps.label: Python builds the customers list with all 8 names.
The for loop runs top_up(name) once for each name in customers, in order.
The for loop stops automatically right after Adjoa, the 8th name.
change_given and coins_used both start at 0.
The while loop checks change_given < 13 before every round, adding 2 and incrementing coins_used each time it's still true.
Once change_given reaches 14, the condition change_given < 13 is false, so the while loop stops.

predictOutput.question: After this code finishes running, what are the final values of coins_used and change_given?

options.text: coins_used is 7 and change_given is 14
coins_used is 6 and change_given is 13
options.hint: Since change_given jumps by 2 each time, can it ever land exactly on 13?

options.text: coins_used is 8 and change_given is 16
options.hint: Try tracing change_given step by step from 0, checking the condition before each add.

edgeCase.question: What happens if the line change_given += 2 is accidentally left out of the while loop's body?

options.text: change_given stays 0 forever, so the loop never stops
Python notices nothing changed and exits the loop after one round
options.hint: If nothing inside the loop body ever changes change_given, will the condition change_given < 13 ever become false on its own?

stage5.practicePrompt: Efua needs a loop to text each of her 5 fixed suppliers and a separate loop to hand back coins until a refund reaches 7 cedis, using the right tool for each job.
stage5.practiceTemplate:
suppliers = ["Yaa", "Kwesi", "Nana", "Esi", "Fiifi"]
___ supplier in suppliers:
    send_text(supplier)

refund_given = 0
___ refund_given < 7:
    refund_given += 1

practiceTokens.hint: What if Efua doesn't know ahead of time how many coins it will take to reach the refund?

applyCheck.prompt: Which situation actually needs one of these two repeating tools, rather than something simpler?

options.text: A radio host keeps announcing raffle numbers one by one until someone finally shouts that they've won, with no idea in advance how many numbers that will take.
A shop clerk prints a single receipt for one sale.
options.hint: Is anything here actually repeating, or is it just one action happening once?

options.text: A courier already knows he has exactly 3 packages today and drives to each address once.
options.hint: With only 3 stops known in advance, could you just write out the 3 steps by hand instead of setting up a repeating tool?

caseStudies.scaleReflection: If Kofi's supplier list grew from 5 to 500, and refunds could still stop at any random coin, would you still trust a for loop for the list and a while loop for the refund, or would something about your reasoning need to change?
